title.en: Print Culture and the Modern World
The book that changed a mind

text.en: Imagine a world without books, newspapers or posters. Everything was copied by hand. Then printing arrived and ideas began to travel faster than ever.

Printing began in East Asia. Woodblock printing in China and Japan produced books and Marco Polo carried the technique to Italy.
Around 1448 Johann Gutenberg developed the printing press in Strasbourg, with metal types. The first book he printed was the Bible.
Printing made books cheap and led to a reading public. It spread new ideas, such as Martin Luther's 95 Theses of 1517 which spurred the Protestant Reformation.
The Church tried to control print through an Index of Prohibited Books. The miller Menocchio was punished for his reading of the Bible.
In the eighteenth century novels and newspapers became popular. Penny chapbooks carried cheap tales and almanacs.
In India, printing came with the Portuguese missionaries, and from the 1800s newspapers like the Bengal Gazette and Sambad Kaumudi appeared.
The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 allowed the government to censor reports in Indian language papers.
Reformers and nationalists used print to spread ideas on caste, women and freedom. Women wrote and read, and cheap prints made visual culture popular.
